pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Pompeii & Vesuvius — a Roman city buried by the AD 79 eruption of Mount Vesuvius, preserved under volcanic ash, and rediscovered by archaeologists centuries later.

- **Standards — UK (cross-curricular):** This is a bridge topic between **Geography** (KS2 volcanoes) and **History** (the Roman world / an aspect of history beyond 1066; Romans commonly taught at KS2). It uses a historical case to make eruption power and preservation concrete; it is not a KS2 science requirement.

- **Standards — US (NGSS/social studies):** No science PE; connects informally to **2-ESS1-1** (some Earth events happen quickly) and to social-studies history-of-place. The science value is 'eruptions are powerful and change the landscape' made vivid through a real event. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Power of Eruptions', 'What Is a Volcano', and (soft) 'Inside a Volcano'. Deliver the narrative — Vesuvius erupted, ash buried Pompeii, the ash PRESERVED the city (buildings, objects, even the shapes of people as voids later cast in plaster), and archaeologists uncovered it and learned about Roman daily life. The science-history hinge: rapid burial by ash both destroyed and preserved, which is why a 2,000-year-old town survives as a snapshot. Handle the human loss sensitively and age-appropriately.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete narrative + observation). Children engage strongly with the story and the plaster casts; the subtle idea is that destruction and preservation happened together. Success = retell that Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in ash, explain that the ash preserved the city, and describe how archaeologists uncovered it and what it teaches us.
bestPractices: Tell it as a true story with a clear arc (ordinary Roman day → eruption → burial → rediscovery), which anchors the abstract 'eruptions are powerful' in a real place.
Make the preservation paradox explicit and age-appropriate: the same ash that buried the city also FROZE it in time, which is why we can see Roman streets, bread, and graffiti today.

Explain the plaster casts carefully and gently: ash hardened around people/animals; bodies decayed leaving voids; archaeologists poured plaster into the voids to recover their shapes — a powerful, sensitive image of real people.
Use eyewitness testimony (Pliny the Younger's letters describe the column of ash) to connect science with primary historical evidence.
Frame archaeology as evidence-based detective work: what everyday objects and buildings reveal about how Romans actually lived — links to History.
keyRepresentations: Story-arc sequence: Roman Pompeii → Vesuvius erupts → city buried in ash → rediscovered and excavated
Then/now paired view of a Pompeii street (buried vs excavated)
The plaster-cast process: void in ash → plaster poured → recovered shape
Pliny the Younger's eyewitness description of the eruption column (primary source)
commonMisconceptions: Pompeii was destroyed by flowing lava (it was buried by ash, pumice and hot ash surges — not a lava flow).
The plaster casts are the actual preserved bodies (they are plaster poured into voids left where bodies decayed in the hardened ash).
Everyone escaped / no one was affected (many escaped, but the disaster caused real loss — handle sensitively).
Pompeii was found recently/by accident only (it was gradually rediscovered and deliberately excavated by archaeologists over centuries).
Volcanoes only destroy (here the eruption also preserved an entire city, teaching us about Roman life).

learn.summary: Learners aged 7–9 explore the story of Pompeii and Mount Vesuvius: an ordinary Roman city buried by the AD 79 eruption, preserved under volcanic ash, and later excavated by archaeologists. The central insight is the preservation paradox — the same rapid ash burial that destroyed the city also sealed and 'froze' it, which is why a 2,000-year-old town survives as a snapshot of Roman daily life. Activities centre on in-role dialogue (eyewitness and archaeologist), then/now image exploration, event sequencing, a hands-on burial-and-excavation model, and an optional 3D reconstruction. Key factual corrections to carry throughout: Pompeii was buried by ash, pumice and hot ash surges (not a lava flow), and the famous 'bodies' are plaster casts poured into hollows left where bodies decayed in the hardened ash — not petrified real bodies. Human loss is handled sensitively and non-graphically.

activities.title: Interview an eyewitness and an archaeologist
feedback: If a learner says the casts are real bodies turned to stone, respond gently: the bodies decayed away and left hollow, body-shaped spaces in the hardened ash; archaeologists later poured plaster into those hollows to recover the shapes.
If a learner says lava flowed over Pompeii, clarify that it was falling ash and pumice and hot ash-and-gas surges that buried the city, not a river of molten lava.
If a learner describes only destruction, prompt: what happened to the streets, bread and writing under all that ash? Draw out that the sealing ash is why so much survived.
Affirm good questions and vivid retelling; invite the learner to ask one more thing they are curious about.
activities.rationale: A human, historical topic is carried by felt experience and an evidence trail. An in-role eyewitness (grounded in Pliny's real letters) and an expert let a child ask open questions and hear persona-grounded answers, which can make the preservation paradox land through story rather than assertion. Characters should proactively offer vivid, age-appropriate detail and invite questions so a child who does not know what to ask is still carried through the arc. This is a proposed approach; the cited sources establish the facts and the existence of the primary source, not that dialogue outperforms other media.
sourceClaims: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash and pumice (not a lava flow); the city was preserved and later excavated by archaeologists.
Pliny the Younger wrote eyewitness letters describing the eruption column and events, a key primary source.
The 'bodies' of Pompeii are plaster casts made by pouring plaster into voids left in the hardened ash where victims decayed.
learnerActions: Talk in role with Pliny the Younger, who watched Vesuvius erupt from across the bay, asking questions like 'What did you see?', 'What did it sound like?', 'Were you frightened?', 'What was the cloud shaped like?'
Switch to talking with an archaeologist excavating Pompeii and ask 'Why are there people-shaped holes in the ash?', 'How do you know how the Romans lived?', 'Why did so much survive?'
Say back, in your own words, what buried the city and why the archaeologist's answer means the casts are not real bodies
activities.intendedInsight: The eruption both destroyed Pompeii and preserved it: the ash that buried the city also sealed buildings, objects and the shapes of people, which is exactly why we can learn about Roman daily life today.

activities.title: Then-and-now Pompeii street
feedback: When a learner taps an object, name what it reveals (e.g. a bakery shows Romans baked bread much as we do; graffiti shows people wrote on walls).
When a learner taps a cast, restate the void→plaster→shape process so they do not mistake it for a preserved body.
If a learner thinks the city was found recently or purely by accident, note it was gradually rediscovered and deliberately excavated by archaeologists over centuries.
activities.rationale: A static, curated scene fits the 'here is what survived' half of the topic and supports exploration of the preserved city and the cast method. It is a complement to, not a replacement for, the eyewitness/questioning dimension; the tap-to-reveal panels make the Roman-life evidence concrete. Recognising or tapping an object alone does not elicit the learner's own explanation of the paradox, so pair it with a prompt to explain in their own words.
sourceClaims: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash and pumice (not a lava flow); the city was preserved and later excavated by archaeologists.
The 'bodies' of Pompeii are plaster casts made by pouring plaster into voids left in the hardened ash where victims decayed.
learnerActions: Use a then/now view of the same Pompeii street — the buried, unexcavated state versus the excavated ruins today — sliding or tapping to compare the two states (if any reconstruction image is offered, it is clearly labelled as an artist's reconstruction, not the surviving remains)
Tap preserved features — a bakery, a cart, graffiti on a wall — to reveal what each tells us about how Romans actually lived
Tap a plaster cast to see, gently, how it was made: void in the hardened ash → plaster poured in → recovered shape
Look up to see Vesuvius looming over the bay and connect the mountain to what happened
activities.intendedInsight: A curated set of surviving everyday objects and buildings shows that a whole city was sealed in time, letting us read Roman daily life directly from what the ash preserved.

activities.title: Sequence the story and sort the clues
feedback: If the learner chooses 'lava', correct to ash, pumice and hot ash surges and ask them to say what is different about a lava flow.
If the sequence places rediscovery before burial, retell the arc: the city lived, was buried, then was found and dug up much later.
For a correct match, reinforce the reasoning ('because the ash sealed the bakery, we can see how bread was made').
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching consolidate factual recall and the key ash-vs-lava correction. This kind of task checks and reinforces the story and can confirm classification of finds, but it does not by itself carry the narrative or emotional weight, nor does it on its own elicit the learner's own explanation of the paradox; it may therefore be most useful as consolidation following the dialogue or image exploration and paired with an explain-in-your-own-words prompt. Efficacy of any ordering is untested.
sourceClaims: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash and pumice (not a lava flow); the city was preserved and later excavated by archaeologists.
learnerActions: Put the events in order: ordinary Roman Pompeii → Vesuvius erupts → city buried in ash → rediscovered → excavated by archaeologists
Answer: 'What buried Pompeii — lava or ash?' and explain the difference between a lava flow and falling/surging ash
Match preserved objects to what they tell us about Roman life (e.g. bakery → bread; cart → travel/trade; graffiti → writing)
After ordering/matching, explain in your own words how the eruption both destroyed and preserved the city
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the correct sequence of events and the ash-not-lava distinction, and connect specific finds to specific conclusions about Roman daily life.

activities.title: Bury it, then dig it up
feedback: If a learner expects to find nothing intact, point out that the covering kept the lower layers protected.
Connect the activity back to the real event: this is why archaeologists found whole streets and objects at Pompeii.
Remind learners this is a model: real burial involved hot, dangerous ash and pumice and the loss of life, handled with care.
activities.rationale: A burial-and-excavation model can make burial-and-preservation visible and physical. The topic's main value is human and historical rather than a physical system to manipulate, so this is a modest complement to the narrative, not its core.
sourceClaims: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash and pumice (not a lava flow); the city was preserved and later excavated by archaeologists.
learnerActions: Watch or model ash accumulating over a small city (e.g. with a toy/model town and a dry, pourable material, or an on-screen simulation) until the buildings are covered
Carefully 'excavate' layer by layer to reveal the preserved streets and objects underneath

Describe what you observe: the covering hid the model town and also kept what was underneath in place for you to find (at the real Pompeii, many roofs fell in under the weight of the pumice, but streets, walls and many objects were kept where they were)
activities.intendedInsight: Rapid burial by ash physically seals and protects what lies beneath, so careful digging later can recover it — a concrete model of how destruction and preservation happened together.

activities.title: Walk a reconstructed Pompeii street (optional immersion extension)
feedback: Remind learners the reconstruction is an informed artist's version, not surviving remains; the real evidence is the excavated ruins and preserved objects.
Connect back: what survived in the ruins and casts is exactly why archaeologists can reconstruct the street at all.
If a learner treats the reconstruction as proof of a detail, ask what surviving object or building that idea is actually based on.
activities.rationale: A walkable 3D reconstruction can be immersive, but it is a costly build whose core insight — what survived and why — is already delivered by the dialogue and then/now image; it is retained as a distinct optional extension rather than core content. Efficacy is untested and it must not be mistaken for the surviving site.
sourceClaims: Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash and pumice (not a lava flow); the city was preserved and later excavated by archaeologists.
learnerActions: Explore a 3D reconstruction of a Pompeii street as it may have looked in Roman times — clearly labelled as an artist's reconstruction, not a photograph of the surviving remains
Then view the same street as excavated ruins to compare the once-living city with what actually survived
Describe one thing the reconstruction helped you picture about Roman daily life, and one thing you can only learn from the real surviving objects
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a street first as a living Roman place and then as ruins helps connect the human city to the evidence that survived; the reconstruction is an informed interpretation, while the ruins and preserved objects are the real evidence.

constraints: Handle the human loss sensitively and age-appropriately (7–9 years): keep content non-graphic, acknowledge that many escaped but there was real loss, and avoid dwelling on distressing detail.

Correct two persistent misconceptions explicitly: Pompeii was buried by ash/pumice/hot ash surges, not a lava flow; and the famous 'bodies' are plaster casts poured into voids left by decayed bodies, not petrified real people.

Avoid implying volcanoes 'only destroy' — here the same eruption preserved an entire city; and avoid implying Pompeii was found purely by accident or only recently (it was gradually rediscovered and deliberately excavated over centuries).

Any artist's reconstruction of Pompeii (in a then/now image or a 3D scene) must be clearly labelled as a reconstruction and kept distinct from the excavated ruins and preserved objects, which are the actual surviving evidence.

Ordering/matching tasks and tap-to-reveal panels check and reinforce facts and can confirm classification, but do not, on their own, elicit the learner's own explanation of the destroy-and-preserve paradox; pair them with a prompt that asks the learner to explain it in their own words.
The burial/excavation activity is a model: it shows sealing and recovery but is not a safe or literal depiction of a real eruption; state this to learners.

This is a cross-curricular bridge topic (KS2 History: the Roman world; KS2 Geography: volcanoes) used to make eruption power and preservation vivid through a real event; it is not a KS2 science requirement, and it connects only informally to US NGSS 2-ESS1-1 (some Earth events happen quickly).

In-role characters should proactively offer detail and invite questions so a child who does not know what to ask is still guided through the arc; Pliny's account should stay grounded in his real letters.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All four listed sources are marked verified:false in the original, so treat them as unconfirmed; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's sources[].claim and underpin the factual content taught in each activity; citation does not establish that any activity here was empirically tested or is comparatively more effective than another medium.

The original framed conversation as uniquely able to deliver 'what a diagram cannot' and claimed a quiz/image 'loses' to it and 'can't carry' narrative/emotional weight. These have been reframed as affordances (dialogue suits open questioning and felt experience; curated images suit surveying what survived) rather than proven universal superiority; efficacy is untested.

The original's 3D walkable reconstruction alternative has been retained as a distinct optional immersion extension rather than folded away, with explicit labelling that reconstructions are not the surviving ruins; it remains an untested proposal.

The original pedagogy listed prior micro-topics as prerequisites ('Power of Eruptions', 'What Is a Volcano', and a soft 'Inside a Volcano'); their internal IDs were removed, but this activity set is intended to follow them.

Source claims were preserved as written: the AD 79 date, ash/pumice burial, Pliny the Younger's eyewitness letters, and the void→plaster cast method are standard but were not independently re-verified in this rewrite.

Diagnostic-derived language ('ash set hard around the people; the bodies later decayed away, leaving hollow body-shaped spaces') is reproduced in feedback as-is; it matches common museum/archaeological descriptions and was not re-checked against a source, and does not separate ash-fall from pyroclastic-surge deposits.

probeDeeper: If the bodies decayed away, how did we end up with body-shaped figures to look at?
How can burying a city in ash both destroy it and help us learn about it centuries later?
Was it flowing lava or ash that buried Pompeii? What's the difference?
What can archaeologists learn about Roman daily life from a city sealed so suddenly?
assess.correctAnswer: Not quite — they aren't turned-to-stone bodies. When Vesuvius erupted, ash buried Pompeii and set hard around the people; the bodies later decayed away, leaving hollow body-shaped spaces in the ash. Archaeologists poured plaster into those hollows to make the shapes we see. The eruption both destroyed the city (killed people, buried it) and preserved it (the ash sealed buildings and everyday life for centuries until it was dug up).

errorPatterns.pattern: The body shapes are the real people turned to stone
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the bodies decayed, leaving hollows in the hardened ash; plaster was poured in to form the casts.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the real bodies, turned to stone by the volcano.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the casts are petrified or fossilised bodies.

errorPatterns.pattern: Molten lava flowed over and buried Pompeii
errorPatterns.nextMove: It was falling ash and hot ash-and-gas (pyroclastic) that buried Pompeii, not a lava flow.
errorPatterns.distractor: Molten lava flowed over the city and buried it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a lava flow covered the city.

errorPatterns.pattern: The eruption only destroyed — nothing good came of it (misses the preservation paradox)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The sealing ash is exactly why so much survived for archaeologists to study.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes destruction only; can't see how it preserved evidence.

responseLevels.gap: Retells only 'a volcano buried Pompeii'; thinks the casts are real turned-to-stone bodies.
responseLevels.full: Explains the casts were made by pouring plaster into body-shaped hollows left in the ash, and how the eruption both destroyed and preserved the city (ash sealing daily life for archaeologists) — distinguishing ash burial from a lava flow.
responseLevels.partial: Retells the story and knows the ash preserved things but believes the casts are the bodies, or can't articulate the destroy-and-preserve paradox.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the Pompeii museum you can see human body shapes. A friend says, 'Those are the actual bodies of the people, turned to stone by the volcano.' Is that right? What are those shapes really, and how did the eruption both destroy AND preserve the city?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can retell 'Vesuvius buried Pompeii in ash' yet believe the casts are petrified bodies and miss the destroy-and-preserve paradox. Asking what the shapes really are AND how the eruption both destroyed and preserved forces the void→cast method and the double effect — separating retelling from understanding.
